questions.question: If you add up all the deviations (value − mean) of a dataset, what do you always get?
questions.explanation: Values above the mean are balanced exactly by values below it, so the raw deviations always sum to 0. That is why we square them before summing.

questions.question: Standard deviation is measured in...
options: The same units as the data
questions.explanation: Variance is in squared units, but taking the square root brings the standard deviation back to the original units (points, cm, dollars).

questions.question: Scores 72, 85, 90, 68, 95 have mean 82 and a sum of squared deviations of 538. What is the sample variance?
questions.explanation: A sample divides by n − 1 = 4: 538 ÷ 4 = 134.5. (538 ÷ 5 = 107.6 would be the population-style divisor. The square root of 134.5, about 11.6, is the standard deviation.)

questions.question: Why does a sample variance divide by n − 1 instead of n?
options: To make the number bigger for no reason
Dividing by n tends to underestimate the population variance, and n − 1 corrects it
questions.explanation: Sample values sit closer to their own mean than to the true population mean, so dividing by n gives a number that is too small on average. In the lesson's simulation, dividing by n averaged about 80 versus the true 100, while n − 1 averaged about 100.

questions.question: You add 10 to every value in a dataset. What happens to the standard deviation?
questions.explanation: Shifting all values moves the mean by the same amount, so every distance from the mean is unchanged. Spread ignores shifts. (Multiplying by 2 would double the SD.)

questions.question: A dataset is strongly skewed with a few extreme values. Which spread measure pairs best with the median?
questions.explanation: The IQR ignores the extremes, as the median does. The standard deviation squares every deviation, so extreme values inflate it.
